title: Irrigation service reports and maintenance contracts
audience: Irrigation business owners, office staff and technicians who write service reports, sell maintenance agreements and manage recurring irrigation work.
learningOutcomes: Write a service report that records what was checked, what was done, what was referred and what the client needs to decide.
Design a maintenance agreement with defined visits, inclusions, exclusions and approval steps.
Price maintenance agreements and repair follow-up so that revenue reflects the work and the risk.
Describe water-saving outcomes only as far as the measurements support them.

instruction.heading: Why service reports create repeat work
instruction.body: A clear service report is the most useful sales tool an irrigation business has. It shows the client what was found, what was done and what needs attention, and it builds trust that the business is looking after the system. A client who receives a report with a list of zone faults, a referral for a supply-side leak and a suggested seasonal schedule is far more likely to book the next visit and to approve the referred work. A vague report that says the system was checked does the opposite. The report should be written for the client to read, not only for the technician, and it should separate what the business can do from what needs a licence holder.

instruction.heading: Writing the service report
instruction.body: Structure the report in the same order each time so that clients learn to read it. Start with the property, the date, the technician and the zones tested. Record the run results for each zone, the faults found with photographs taken with consent, and the actions taken on site. Then list the referrals, each with the reason and the licence class needed, and the items that need the client's decision, such as a head replacement that is in scope but has a cost. End with the schedule that is in place and the next recommended visit. Keep the language plain. Avoid promises such as the system will be leak-free or will save a set percentage of water, unless the measurements in the report support them. A report that is honest about limits is more credible than one that promises everything.

instruction.heading: Designing a maintenance agreement
instruction.body: A maintenance agreement sets out the visits, the inclusions and the exclusions, and the approval steps for extra work. A common structure is a seasonal check at the start of the warm and cool seasons, with a schedule review and a report. Inclusions may be the zone run test, the filter clean, the schedule adjustment and the service report. Exclusions should be listed clearly: supply-side and plumbing repairs, electrical work, backflow testing and any repair that needs a licence holder. The agreement should say how extra work is approved, typically by a written quote from the business or its licensed partner, and how a visit is rescheduled for weather or access problems. Do not describe the agreement as a licence, a certification or a guarantee of a leak-free system.

instruction.heading: Pricing and referral revenue
instruction.body: Price maintenance agreements from the work they contain. Build the price from the time for each visit, travel, the report time, a materials allowance for filters, washers and minor parts, and an allowance for the risk that a system in poor condition will need more attention. Set a separate price for extra in-scope work, such as a head replacement, and make sure the client sees the difference between the agreement and extra work. Referral work for licence holders is not revenue the business earns from its own labour. Where the business has an arrangement with a licence holder, record the arrangement in writing, state how the client will be billed for the licensed work, and make clear who carries out the work. Do not invent a commission or fee arrangement; check the state or territory rules first.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor should check the report, the agreement and the pricing against the work done. A competent office or crew lead can show how each price was built, identify the exclusions, and explain how a referral is handed over to a licence holder. Escalate any report that describes licensed work as completed by the business, any agreement that includes supply-side or electrical work without a licensed partner, and any claim about water savings that the measurements do not support.

procedure: Complete the service report in the standard order, with the zone results, faults, actions and photographs taken with consent.
List each referral with the reason, the licence class needed and the client's next step.
Mark items that need the client's decision, with a quote and a deadline where the business sets one.
Write the agreement with visits, inclusions, exclusions, approval steps and a rescheduling rule.
Price the agreement from visit time, travel, materials allowance, report time and the risk of the system's age and condition.
Set the approved referral process, including the licence holder's contact and the handover of photographs and notes.
Give the client the report and the agreement, and ask for confirmation of the decisions they have made.
File the report, the agreement, the approval and the referral record in the client file.

workedExamples.situation: A client has a maintenance agreement. At the autumn visit the technician finds a zone with two blocked drippers and a supply-side leak near the backflow device.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you write the report and handle the follow-up?
workedExamples.reasoning: Record the blocked drippers and the action taken, and list them as in-scope work with a quote if the agreement excludes repairs. Record the supply-side leak as a referral to a licence holder, with the location, the symptoms and the photographs taken with consent. Tell the client the referral is needed and that the business will not carry out the supply-side repair. Ask for a decision on the in-scope work and confirm the next visit.

workedExamples.situation: A prospective client asks for a written promise that a new system will save 40 per cent of its water bill.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not promise a percentage saving. The saving depends on the existing system, the plants, the schedule and the client's use, and there are no measurements to support a figure. Offer to measure the existing use and to report the change after a set period, and state that the report will show what the measurements support.

equipmentAndPpe: Service report template with standard sections
Maintenance agreement template with inclusions and exclusions
Camera or phone for photographs, with consent
Pricing worksheet for visits, reports and referrals

commonErrors.error: Writing a report that says the system works and leaves out the faults found.
commonErrors.prevention: Record every zone result and every fault, and separate in-scope work from referrals.

commonErrors.error: Including supply-side or electrical repairs in the agreement as if the business can do them.
commonErrors.prevention: Exclude licensed work from the agreement, and offer a referral to a licence holder instead.

commonErrors.error: Promising a water-saving percentage or a leak-free system.
commonErrors.prevention: Report only what the measurements support, and state the limits of the inspection.

commonErrors.error: Pricing the agreement by the number of zones alone.
commonErrors.prevention: Price from visit time, travel, reporting time, materials allowance and the age and condition of the system.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The business must not present a referral to a licence holder as work it has completed, and must not claim a licence or authority the business does not hold. In New South Wales, urban irrigation water plumbing is a licensed category covering connection to a water main (page updated 31 July 2026).
Water-saving and environmental claims must be supported by evidence.

qualityStandard: Every service report lists the zones tested, the results, the faults, the actions taken and the referrals.
Every maintenance agreement lists visits, inclusions, exclusions, the approval step for extra work and the rescheduling rule.
Every price is built from a recorded worksheet.
No claim is made that the measurements do not support.
documentationEvidence: Signed service reports for each visit.
Signed maintenance agreement with exclusions and approval steps.
Referral records with the licence holder named and the handover recorded.
Pricing worksheet for the agreement and any extra work.
summary: A clear service report is the basis for repeat work and approvals.
Maintenance agreements set out visits, inclusions and exclusions, and keep licensed work with licence holders.
Price from the work, the risk and the reporting time, not from the number of zones alone.
Make no water-saving or leak-free claim that the measurements do not support.

knowledgeChecks.question: A service report finds a supply-side leak near the backflow device. How should it be recorded?
options: As completed, since the technician isolated the zone and the water was stopped on the day and the client was happy with the result
As a referral to a licence holder, with the location, symptoms, photographs taken with consent and the client's next step.
Left out of the report so the client is not worried by the leak finding at the time of the visit and the job

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks for a written promise of a 40 per cent water saving. What is the correct response?
options: Agree and put the figure in the agreement, since the client has asked for a firm number to sign
Say the saving depends on the weather and do nothing else, since that covers the business fully
Do not promise a percentage. Offer to measure current use and report what the measurements support.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which item should be an exclusion in a maintenance agreement?
options: Supply-side and plumbing repairs, which need a licence holder.
Seasonal schedule review, done once each year with the client
Filter cleaning during a scheduled visit to the site each season
